claims.text: Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 is a phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloy.
Introducing approximately 1 at.% Y during arc melting will improve the alloy's glass-forming ability.
Introducing approximately 1 at.% Y will enhance the thermal stability of the amorphous state.
The beneficial effect of Y depends on its uniform distribution in the alloy.
A narrow Y concentration range around 1 at.% is expected to be beneficial.
Excessive Y concentration may produce unwanted secondary phases.
Poorly distributed Y may lead to phase separation or unwanted secondary phases.
Y atoms introduce atomic-size mismatch and electronic disparities.
The size mismatch and electronic disparities caused by Y induce local packing frustration.
Y-induced local packing frustration hinders the formation of crystalline nuclei.
Y microalloying increases local structural disorder and raises the nucleation energy barrier during rapid solidification.
The increased nucleation barrier delays premature crystallization and promotes formation and retention of an amorphous structure.
Relative to the Y-free baseline, the Y-doped alloy will have a lower critical cooling rate for complete amorphization.
Relative to the Y-free baseline, the Y-doped alloy will have a higher DSC crystallization-onset temperature.
Rapid quenching by melt-spinning at approximately 10^6 K/s is a condition under which the intervention is expected to operate.
Inadequate homogenization may limit or eliminate the beneficial effect of Y.
The optimal Y concentration and the magnitude of improvement remain unknown.

contradictions.description: Uniform Y distribution is stated as a prerequisite, and nonuniform distribution is identified as an out-of-boundary condition that may generate secondary phases; nevertheless, secondary phases caused by nonuniform distribution are also declared to falsify the hypothesis. A failed prerequisite therefore counts simultaneously as being outside the hypothesis's conditions and as a decisive falsification.
